group.passage:
In the 1870s, a library reader often could not simply walk to the shelf for chemistry or history. In most libraries, a book’s number recorded the room, the case, and the shelf where it happened to stand, not what it was about. Some collections were arranged in the order the books had arrived, and others only by size, so a reader hunting for one subject might have to scan every book of the right height. Worse, whenever the space set aside for a subject filled up, books had to be moved and given new numbers.
Melvil Dewey, a student at Amherst College who worked in its library, found this waste maddening. He later said he had visited more than 50 libraries and had been shocked by the time and money they spent renumbering books. By his own account, the answer came to him one Sunday during a long sermon by the college president, and he jumped in his seat and nearly shouted “Eureka!” On May 8, 1873, the 21-year-old presented the library committee with a plan to rearrange the collection by subject.
His key idea was to number subjects rather than shelves. He divided all knowledge into ten main classes, split each class into ten divisions and each division into ten sections, giving 1,000 categories in all. A book’s number now showed what it was about and where it belonged among related books, so new titles could be slipped in without changing any old numbers. Because the numbers worked as decimals, a crowded category could always be divided again simply by adding digits. When the scheme appeared in 1876, in a booklet of fewer than fifty pages that did not even carry his name, many librarians found it far too detailed.
Not everyone gives Dewey all the credit. His biographer Wayne Wiegand argues that Dewey’s real talent lay in combining and adjusting the best parts of other people’s schemes. Still, the combination traveled far. Today Dewey numbers remain more common in public and school libraries than in large research libraries, and in 1929 the librarian Liu Guojun drew on the same plan of ten classes divided by tens for a system that Taiwan’s National Central Library revised as recently as 2007.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage is developed?

options.A: It describes a problem, explains one student’s answer to it, and then weighs his credit and influence.
options.B: It compares two ways of arranging books and argues that the newer one is better in every way.
options.C: It follows Dewey’s life from his school years to his old age.
options.D: It explains, step by step, how a librarian gives a number to a new book.

questions.stem: Under the system used in most libraries before Dewey’s, what would most likely happen if a library received a large number of new books on chemistry?

options.A: Readers would be able to find chemistry books more quickly than before.
options.B: The new books would be sorted into ten main classes.
options.C: The new books would get numbers showing what they were about.
options.D: Some books already on the shelves might need new places and new numbers.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true about the booklet Dewey published in 1876?

options.A: It was printed under Dewey’s name and ran to more than fifty pages.
options.B: It offered more categories than many librarians felt they needed.
options.C: It gave each book a number showing the room and shelf where it stood.
options.D: It was the first plan Dewey ever put before the library committee.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention Wayne Wiegand?

options.A: To suggest that the story about the sermon was made up later.
options.B: To explain why Dewey’s name was left off the 1876 booklet.
options.C: To give a more balanced view of how original Dewey’s system was.
options.D: To show that most libraries have since replaced Dewey’s system.

evidence: Worse, whenever the space set aside for a subject filled up, books had to be moved and given new numbers.

option_notes_zh.C: 範圍不對：文中只寫到杜威在 Amherst 求學期間（1873 年）到 1876 年發表方案，沒有寫他的晚年。
option_notes_zh.D: 答非所問：文中說明的是分類法的原理（依主題、十進細分），不是圖書館員替新書編號的操作步驟。

translation_zh.text:
在 1870 年代，圖書館的讀者常常沒辦法直接走到化學或歷史的書架前。在大多數圖書館，一本書的編號記錄的是它碰巧放在哪個房間、哪個書櫃、哪一層書架，而不是它的內容。有些館藏依書到館的先後排列，有些只依大小排列，所以想找某個主題的讀者，可能得把同樣高度的書一本本看過。更糟的是，每當某個主題預留的空間放滿了，書就得搬動，並換上新的編號。
梅爾維爾‧杜威是 Amherst 學院的學生，在學校圖書館打工，他覺得這種浪費令人抓狂。他後來說，他參觀過 50 多座圖書館，對它們花在重新編號上的時間和金錢感到震驚。據他自己的說法，答案是在某個星期天、院長一場冗長的講道中浮現的，他在座位上一躍，差點大喊「我找到了！」1873 年 5 月 8 日，這位 21 歲的年輕人向圖書館委員會提出一份依主題重新排列館藏的計畫。
他的關鍵想法是替主題編號，而不是替書架編號。他把所有知識分成十個大類，每個大類再分成十個小類，每個小類再分成十個細目，一共 1,000 個類目。如今書的編號顯示的是它的內容，以及它在相關書籍之間的位置，所以新書可以直接插進去，不必更動任何舊編號。由於這些編號當作小數使用，擁擠的類目只要加上數字，隨時都能再往下細分。1876 年這套方案問世時，印成一本不到五十頁、連作者姓名都沒有的小冊子，許多圖書館員覺得它實在太過細瑣。
並不是每個人都把功勞全歸給杜威。他的傳記作者韋恩‧威根德認為，杜威真正的本事在於結合並調整別人方案中最好的部分。儘管如此，這個組合流傳得很遠。今天，杜威的編號在公共圖書館和學校圖書館仍比在大型研究圖書館常見；1929 年，圖書館學者劉國鈞也借用了同樣「十大類、逐層以十細分」的架構編成一套分類法，台灣的國家圖書館直到 2007 年都還在修訂它。

open_tasks.prompt: Dewey numbered subjects, not shelves. In 1–2 English sentences, explain why this made a librarian’s work easier when many new books arrived.
reference_answers: Because a book’s number showed its subject rather than its spot on a shelf, new books could be put among related books without changing the numbers of the old ones.
When a shelf filled up, librarians could simply move the books along, since the numbers did not depend on where the books stood.
